newsitem.title: USA: Illinois tollway target of legislative hearing.
newsitem.headline: Illinois tollway target of legislative hearing.

text.p: A chorus of criticism aimed at the Illinois State Toll Highway Authority surfaced Monday at an Illinois House committee hearing on reforming the bond-issuing agency.

Individuals and citizen and environmental groups testified to the need for greater accountability at the authority. Much of the criticism was sparked by plans to eventually extend the tollway system in northeastern Illinois by 75 miles at a cost of more than $2 billion.

"It's the most thorough and comprehensive look the tollway authority has had for quite some time," said State Rep. Jeff Schoenberg, D-Wilmette, chairman of the House Appropriations and General Services Committee, which held the hearing in Chicago.
Schoenberg said following a second hearing in Springfield on Wednesday House Democrats may begin to move on bills aimed at reforming the toll agency.

State Rep. Lauren Beth Gash, D-Deerfield, the committee's co-chairman, said she has as many as 15 bills in the works that range from turning existing tollways into freeway, to placing more financial constraints on the authority's finances.

One bill would create the post of inspector general for the agency to investigate fraud and financial mismanagement and require the agency to use surplus revenue for road rehabilitation projects before issuing any bonds.
Another measure would subject the agency's annual budget to the the General Assembly's appropriation process.
While Gash said she has unsuccessfully proposed some of the measures before, she believed tollway reforms have "a very good chance this year."

Julian D'Esposito, the tollway authority's chairman, said many of the proposed reforms, like placing the agency's budget into the relm of legislative appropriations, "would change the nature of the authority as a financial entity."
"If the authority is subject to annual appropriations, it is a different kind of credit," he said.
He said the measures could conflict with convenents made with bondholders of outstanding authority debt.

In testimony before the House committee, D'Esposito said Illinois would not have been able to meet or continue to meet its transportation objectives without toll-financed highways given decreases in federal and state road funding.
He also outlined several areas of reform undertaken by the agency itself in the areas of ethics, internal audits and public imput.
